query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A real-time, machine-learning-driven feedback control system that continuously adapts laser power, scan speed, and layer thickness during L-PBF printing will reduce pore formation and geometric inaccuracies in high-entropy-alloy builds, thus improving dimensional precision and tensile integrity over static-parameter processes.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy powder feedstock (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi or CoCrFeNiCu) sized and stored per standard AM procedures, with typical oxygen content (<200 ppm) and humidity control.
generation.intervention: Implement an adaptive, in-situ monitoring and control strategy that utilizes ML models trained on sensor data (e.g., melt-pool imaging, thermal signatures) to dynamically adjust key L-PBF parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, and layer thickness in real time.
generation.conditions: Laser powder bed fusion of CoCrFeMnNi or CoCrFeNiCu alloys at industrial scales (laser power ~100–400 W, scan speeds in the 400–1200 mm/s range, layer thickness 30–50 μm) under standard inert gas environments for oxidation control.
generation.structural_mediator: Stable melt-pool dynamics and reduced local thermal gradients, leading to decreased keyhole and lack-of-fusion defects, minimizing pore nucleation sites and residual stress buildup within the additively manufactured microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Real-time sensor feedback and machine-learning algorithms identify suboptimal thermal and melt-pool conditions at each layer, then rapidly adjust process parameters to maintain optimal energy input and scan rate, reducing defect initiation while maintaining tight dimensional control.
generation.predicted_outcome: Porosity will decrease by as much as half relative to baseline static-parameter builds, and dimensional precision will improve sufficiently to reduce net shape deviations and enhance mechanical properties in tensile loading.
generation.baseline: Standard L-PBF builds rely on fixed or manually tuned parameters, often yielding CoCrFeMnNi(Cu) components with up to ~1–2% porosity and notable geometric deviations.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness may be constrained by the availability and resolution of real-time measurement data and the composition’s intrinsic susceptibility to hot cracking or vigorous melt-pool dynamics. Excessive heat input can exacerbate cracking if not accurately modeled.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements in density and dimensional control will depend on each HEA’s composition and the comprehensiveness of training data used in the ML model. Further validation is needed to confirm the generality of this approach across different process scales.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate identical sets of high-entropy-alloy test components via L-PBF under two conditions: one with real-time ML-driven adaptive control and another with conventional static parameter settings derived from best-practice guidelines. Perform this under strictly identical feedstock, geometry, and environment conditions to isolate the effect of the control system.
measurements: Metrological scans (e.g., 3D optical or CT) to quantify dimensional accuracy relative to the design CAD model
Archimedean or X-ray CT density measurements to assess porosity and detect internal defects
Tensile tests to evaluate mechanical integrity (e.g., yield and ultimate strength, ductility)
Microhardness mapping in cross-sections to verify uniformity of the microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the adaptive ML-controlled group does not show a statistically significant (p ≥ 0.05) reduction in internal pore fraction or an improvement in dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties compared to the static-parameter group, this would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: This study introduces a method that is applicable across various powder materials to predict process conditions that yield a product with a relative density greater than 98% by laser powder bed fusion. We develop an XGBoost model using a dataset comprising material properties of powder and process conditions, and its output, relative density, undergoes a transformation using a sigmoid function to increase accuracy. We deeply examine the relationships between input features and the target value using Shapley additive explanations. Experimental validation with stainless steel 316 L, AlSi10Mg, and Fe60Co15Ni15Cr10 medium entropy alloy powders verifies the method’s reproducibility and transferability. This research contributes to laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing by offering a universally applicable strategy to optimize process conditions. Exploring laser powder bed fusion in manufacturing, the authors demonstrate a machine learning-based method to optimize processing conditions achieving materials with relative density greater than 98% and experimentally verify its generality for multiple distinct powder materials.

Zhu et al. applied the scaling law introduced by Rubenchik et al. to predict melt pool dimensions during the L-PBF AM processes as functions of two dimensionless variables—i.e., p=Daν and B=ΔH23/4πhs, where D, a, and ΔH/hs are the thermal diffusivity, the laser beam radius, and the normalized enthalpy, respectively. This work is fully computational and provides the closest comparison to the framework that we propose in this study. However, while Zhu et al.’s approach employs a single-scaled thermal model and one set of defect criteria for a specific material (a Ni-Ti shape memory alloy), our method integrates three different thermal models and uses twelve different combinations of defect criteria to generate printability maps for an entire alloy system (Cantor alloys), offering a more comprehensive and versatile analysis. Another approach to accelerate printability map production for HTP AM design is applying ML models. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. The printed sample density gradually increases with higher volumetric energy density, achieving densities exceeding 99.0%. However, at higher energy densities, the samples exhibit susceptibility to hot cracking, an issue that cannot be mitigated by adjusting the process parameters. decision.trend: PMC9736672 (2022-12-01) optimized SLM parameters (laser power, scan speed) for CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys, achieving high density and elucidating defect-generation mechanisms. Building on that, PMC12250662 (2025-06-27) further correlated laser power and scan strategies with hot cracking in a CoCrFeNiCu-based HEA, revealing how higher energy densities can improve density but risk crack formation. Despite progress in reducing porosity and improving mechanical performance, fully controlling dimensional precision and residual defects across different builds remains a key technical challenge. The interplay among local thermal gradients, melt pool parameters, and evolving microstructure is still insufficiently understood, motivating a need for more advanced real-time optimization methods.
decision.unsolved: Conventional parameter tuning alone has not eliminated persistent geometric deviation, residual stress, and sub-surface porosity in AM-built high-entropy-alloy parts, limiting mechanical integrity. Achieving consistent high density and surface precision across diverse geometries remains difficult, and advanced in-situ strategies are needed to detect and mitigate defect formation during layer deposition.
decision.lever: Implement a real-time, machine-learning-driven process control system that monitors and adjusts laser power, scan velocity, and layer thickness based on feedback signals (e.g., melt-pool imaging).
decision.why: Prior work shows that careful tuning of powder bed fusion parameters can reduce defects, but controlling dimensional accuracy and microstructure simultaneously across complex geometries remains a challenge. A data-driven approach, with online sensor feedback and predictive modeling, can provide adaptive, fine-grained optimization of thermal conditions and melt-pool stability to minimize void formation, ensure precise dimensions, and enhance mechanical integrity.
